answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Craik’s novel A Life for a Life (London: Hurst and Blackett, 1859), Vol. II, Chapter III (“Her Story”). We confirmed the passage word for word in the Project Gutenberg transcription of that edition; the popular version differs only in punctuation and drops Craik’s italics on “safe.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Vol. II, Chapter III, “Her Story” (numbered Ch. 16 on Wikiquote)
Theodora Johnston, narrator of the “Her Story” chapters

source.excerpt:
Thus ended our little talk: yet it left a pleasant impression. True, the subject was strange enough; my sisters might have been shocked at it; and at my freedom in asking and giving opinions. But oh! the blessing it is to have a friend to whom one can speak fearlessly on any subject; with whom one’s deepest as well as one’s most foolish thoughts come out simply and safely. Oh, the comfort—the inexpressible comfort of feeling safe with a person—having neither to weigh thoughts nor measure words, but pouring them all right out, just as they are, chaff and grain together; certain that a faithful hand will take and sift them, keep what is worth keeping, and then with the breath of kindness blow the rest away.

Somebody must have done a good deal of the winnowing business this afternoon; for in the course of it I gave him as much nonsense as any reasonable man could stand…
trail: 1859 — Craik publishes A Life for a Life in three volumes (Hurst and Blackett). The passage appears in Vol. II, Chapter III, “Her Story” (Project Gutenberg transcription ↗).
1936 — According to Wikiquote, the passage was set out as verse under the title “Friendship” in The Best Loved Poems of the American People (Wikiquote ↗).
2009 — A Usenet thread records that web search results credited the passage to George Eliot, to Craik and to an anonymous “Shoshone” source (alt.english.usage ↗).

Today — Wikiquote lists the passage as a sourced Craik quotation and notes the George Eliot misattribution. Alex Measday’s “Did George Eliot Write This?” also traces it to Craik’s novel (geonius.com ↗).
source.excerptNote: The text follows the Project Gutenberg transcription of Vol. II of the 1859 first edition. The italic safe is Craik’s own emphasis. The popular version drops it and adds a comma after “thoughts.”

author.name: Dinah Maria Mulock Craik
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Dinah Maria Craik, born Dinah Maria Mulock and often credited as “Miss Mulock” or “Mrs. Craik,” was an English novelist and poet. She is best remembered for John Halifax, Gentleman (1857). Her next major novel, A Life for a Life (1859), made more money and may have been more widely read in its day.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The words are Craik’s, but the passage has been passed around for decades without her name. It has been credited to a more famous Victorian novelist, called folk wisdom, and reprinted as a stand-alone poem.

items.why: Wikiquote notes that the passage is misattributed to George Eliot, and Alex Measday’s page on quotes wrongly credited to Eliot says it “was actually written by” Craik (geonius.com ↗; Wikiquote ↗).
A 2009 Usenet thread lists “Anonymous – Shoshone” among the attributions found online. A 2019 reply says a blog that first gave it to the Shoshone was later corrected (alt.english.usage ↗).
In the same thread, a 2019 poster says he found many sites calling it an old Arab proverb but could find no Arabic-language version (alt.english.usage ↗).

The passage is prose from a novel. Wikiquote notes it was set out as verse under the title “Friendship” in The Best Loved Poems of the American People (1936), and Measday notes that people who get the author right often credit the wrong source, a poem called “Friendship” (Wikiquote ↗; geonius.com ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Craik wrote it as prose in her 1859 novel A Life for a Life, Vol. II, Chapter III (Project Gutenberg ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the novel the line is not a free-standing saying about friendship. Theodora Johnston, who narrates the “Her Story” chapters, is looking back on a Sunday-afternoon talk with a man she trusts. She then jokes that “somebody must have done a good deal of the winnowing business this afternoon.” The chaff-and-grain image is a winnowing metaphor, and the novel carries it into the next sentence.

Measday notes that the “strange subject” of that talk was capital punishment, which the minister had preached against that day (geonius.com ↗). Lifted out of that scene, the passage became one of the most widely shared Victorian lines on friendship, usually without Craik’s name.
detailsBody: A blog post quoting Christopher Stevens’s biography of the actor Kenneth Williams says this was the quote that most often closed Williams’s letters. Sometimes he wrote it in full and sometimes just “chaff & grain” (jaywilsonmusic.com ↗).
